Statewide Presumptive Treatment and Diversion for Nonviolent Drug Possession and Low-Level Property Crime: judges must divert eligible first- and second-time offenders (simple possession under state thresholds; theft or shoplifting under $1,000; excluding burglary, robbery, trafficking, and all violent offenses) into a 12–18 month community program pairing medication-assisted treatment, cognitive-behavioral therapy, housing support, and job training; criminal charges are dismissed and records sealed upon completion, with graduated administrative sanctions (e.g., brief jail stays capped at 7 days, increased treatment intensity) for noncompliance and reinstatement of the original sentence only after three failed attempts; funding comes from a statutory reallocation of 20% of projected prison operating cost savings to certified local providers, and outcomes are audited annually on reoffending, employment, and net costs.

Risk-Calibrated Earned-Release and Intensive Supervision: expand earned-time credits up to 30% of sentence for completion of accredited education, vocational, and treatment programs, with eligibility determined by a validated risk/needs assessment and exclusions for designated violent offenses; individuals released early are placed on 12 months of graduated community supervision that begins with GPS monitoring, curfews, and weekly check-ins and steps down to monthly reporting contingent on compliance, with swift-and-certain sanctions (48–72 hour custodial holds) for violations; the state funds 1:35 caseload ratios for parole officers, mandates data-sharing with service providers, and requires independent evaluation of public safety impacts and cost-effectiveness.

Public Safety Capacity and Standards Act: a five-year state program to end chronic prison overcrowding by hiring 15% more correctional staff, imposing a hard cap of 95% design capacity per facility, and authorizing temporary contracts with neighboring jurisdictions; facilities must meet minimum space, programming, and medical staffing standards before accepting new admissions, and the department must prioritize in-prison mental health and addiction services with dedicated clinical units; the act includes a sunset clause and a trigger that suspends admissions for nonviolent technical probation/parole violations when occupancy exceeds the cap, which may increase short-term costs but is intended to stabilize conditions while longer-term sentencing and diversion reforms are implemented.

HM Prison Rehabilitation and Staffing Reform Bill: Mandate minimum prison officer-to-prisoner ratios, raise prison officer pay by 20%, convert large wings into smaller therapeutic units, require every prison to provide accredited education, vocational training, and cognitive-behavioural programs with independent evaluation; create a 12-month post-release resettlement package (housing, employment support, mentoring) for all releases; maintain current sentencing lengths (no early-release quotas) and limit electronic tagging to post-release licence conditions; funded by a multi-year capital program and a dedicated workforce allowance. Tradeoffs include higher upfront costs and temporary disruption during refurbishment.

Presumptive Non-Custodial Sentencing for Low-Level, Non-Violent Offences: Amend the Sentencing Code to create a statutory presumption against custodial sentences under 12 months, replacing them with structured community orders combining unpaid work, fines, curfews, and mandated treatment; judges may depart only with written reasons; cap custody for technical probation breaches at 7 days; increase probation staffing and electronic monitoring capacity; require quarterly compliance reporting to victims and courts; expected to reduce short-term prison receptions. Tradeoffs include higher probation caseloads and risk of non-compliance.

Targeted Decriminalisation and Diversion Pilot: For three years in selected police force areas, reclassify adult simple possession of Class B and C drugs and shop theft under £200 committed without violence as civil infractions handled via on-the-spot fines and mandatory health or social needs assessments, with no criminal record upon completion; require police to offer diversion to treatment and debt/benefits advice; prohibit custodial sentences for these offences during the pilot; independently evaluate impacts on reoffending, public safety, and court backlogs. Tradeoffs include the need for intensive officer training and potential perceptions of reduced deterrence.

Statutory Presumption Against Custody for First-Time Non-Violent Offences: Parliament directs the Sentencing Council to issue binding guidelines creating a presumption of community sentences (rehabilitation activity requirements, unpaid work, accredited programmes, restorative justice) for first-time, non-violent offenders; judges may impose immediate custody only with written reasons citing specific risk of serious harm; successful completion triggers shortened rehabilitation periods and automatic record sealing after 12 months; ring-fenced funding expands programme capacity; tradeoff: requires substantial upfront investment in supervision and services.

Probation Breach and Magistrates’ Flexibility Reform: Legislation authorises probation to impose administrative, graduated sanctions and incentives for first and second technical breaches (extra reporting, curfew extensions, earned-time credits, transport/housing support) without immediate return to court; magistrates gain power to replace custodial sentences up to 12 months with Intensive Rehabilitation Orders combining electronic monitoring, daily reporting, and treatment; mandatory multi-agency case conferences and shared data platforms at sentencing; tradeoff: increases community supervision intensity and surveillance, necessitating safeguards and additional staffing.

Civil Enforcement of Specified Minor Offences Pilot: Reclassify simple drug possession for personal use, shop theft under £200, TV licence evasion, and fare evasion as civil infractions in three police force areas for three years; police issue income-scaled fixed penalties paired with mandated referral to health, debt or employment services; custodial penalties barred for these infractions; establish a Victim Restitution Fund financed by penalties and retailer levies; independent evaluation to assess reoffending, costs and victim outcomes before any nationwide rollout; tradeoff: shifts caseload to civil enforcement and may reduce short-term deterrence without robust compliance mechanisms.

State Presumptive Diversion and Restorative Justice for Low-Level Offenses: Establish a statewide presumption against incarceration for first- and second-time nonviolent misdemeanors and low-level felonies with losses under $1,500; courts must assign a community-based restorative justice plan with victim restitution, 100-200 hours of service, cognitive-behavioral therapy, and job training in lieu of jail. Successful completion seals the record; noncompliance triggers graduated sanctions (fines, intensified programming, and, only after repeated failure, up to 10 consecutive weekend jail days). Exclusions: domestic violence, firearm offenses, and individuals assessed as high risk. Redirect 25% of county jail per-diem savings to certified service providers and victim compensation.

Targeted Crime-Reduction Policing Grants to Lower Prison Admissions: Create a 5-year state grant program that funds municipal hot-spot patrols, problem-oriented policing units, license plate recognition for auto theft, burglary suppression teams, and data analysts, with the explicit goal of reducing index crimes and thereby reducing felony arrests that lead to prison sentences. Grants require performance metrics (crime reduction and prison commitments avoided), body-worn cameras, co-responder mental-health teams, and independent civil-rights audits. Funds may not be used for incarceration capacity. Tradeoffs include higher upfront policing costs and civil-liberty risks mitigated by auditing and transparency.

Intensive Post-Release Supervision with GPS and Earned Discharge: For all individuals released from prison for nonviolent offenses, implement a 12-month community supervision model featuring GPS ankle monitoring for the first 120 days, nightly curfews, weekly in-person reporting, random drug testing when clinically indicated, and mandatory placement in employment or training. Violations receive swift, certain, and fair responses, including 1-3 day jail stays for repeated noncompliance, while sustained compliance earns early discharge after 6-9 months. Expand parole staffing to a 1:40 officer-to-client ratio and provide legal counsel for sanction hearings. Expected benefits include fewer returns to prison for new crimes or technical violations; tradeoffs include surveillance costs and privacy intrusions.

State Presumptive Non-Custodial Sentencing and Sealing for Nonviolent Low-Level Offenses: The state sentencing commission updates guidelines to make community-based sanctions the default for first- and second-time nonviolent offenses with financial loss under $5,000, including mandatory restitution, 200–600 hours of community service, cognitive behavioral therapy, substance-use treatment where indicated, and up to 12 months of supported employment; violations trigger a graduated sanctions ladder before any jail; successful completion leads to automatic conviction sealing; funded by redirecting projected jail operating savings and a 1% court fee surcharge, with independent evaluation of recidivism and costs.

Federal Corrections Workforce and Rehabilitation Modernization Grants: Congress creates a 10-year grant program requiring participating states to raise correctional officer starting pay to at least the regional law-enforcement median, meet safe staffing ratios, and implement Norway-style small housing units with accredited education, industry-recognized vocational training, and trauma-informed therapy inside prisons; grants finance facility renovation to reduce overcrowding, a limited 5–10% earned-time credit tied to completion of intensive programs, and restrict routine use of electronic monitoring for low-risk cases due to poor cost-effectiveness; funding eligibility is contingent on audited reductions in 3-year reoffending rates, not on reducing prison headcount.

Habitual Violent Offender and Victim Protection Act (state level): Establishes mandatory minimum sentences and a 25-years-to-life ‘third violent felony’ provision for enumerated violent crimes; eliminates parole eligibility and plea bargaining for specified serious violent offenses; dedicates funds to add 3,000 secure prison beds and expand victim services and witness protection; requires annual judicial review panels to assess proportionality and a sunset review after 8 years; fiscal note acknowledges higher corrections costs and directs a luxury-goods surcharge and a general-obligation bond issuance to cover near-term capacity expansion.

Sentencing and Diversion Act (UK): Create a statutory presumption against custodial sentences for non-violent, low-harm offences (e.g., theft under £500, simple drug possession, fare evasion), directing courts to use problem-solving courts with mandatory treatment, restorative justice conferencing, unpaid work, curfews with electronic monitoring, and conditional record sealing upon compliance; exclude domestic abuse, stalking, sexual offences, weapon possession, and burglary of a dwelling; require probation-led triage within 14 days; fund by reallocating £300m from prison capital to community treatment and supervision; set outcome metrics (12- and 24-month reoffending, employment, victim satisfaction) and sunset after 5 years unless reauthorised; mitigate risks of net-widening and breach-related custody with graduated sanctions and supportive services.

Serious Violence Sentencing and Parole Reform Bill (UK): Introduce mandatory life sentences with a 30-year minimum tariff for repeat serious violent offenders (e.g., second conviction for homicide, attempted murder, rape, or grievous bodily harm with intent); abolish automatic halfway release for specified violent and sexual offences, moving to a two-thirds release point with Parole Board approval only; expand whole-life orders to murders involving kidnapping or terrorism links; require victims’ rights to be heard at parole; add 1,500 high-security places and fund intensive offence-focused programmes; fiscal impact increases custody costs and crowding pressures but aims to incapacitate high-harm offenders.

Justice Reinvestment and Capacity Cap Programme (UK): Set a statutory target to reduce the average prison population by 20% over five years, with a moratorium on new prison construction and a rolling cap that prioritises capacity for those convicted of serious violent and sexual offences; redirect £1bn in capital and operating savings to scale community mental health, addiction treatment, supported housing, day-reporting centres, and employment pathways in high-incarceration areas; expand earned-release credits up to 30% for completion of accredited education/treatment, and create nationwide pre-charge diversion for low-level drug possession; establish an independent oversight board to publish quarterly progress and reallocate funds; manage public safety risks via risk-based eligibility, electronic monitoring, and swift recall for serious breaches.

England and Wales: Introduce a presumption of non-custodial sentences for first- and second-time non-violent offences with a clinically evidenced addiction component (e.g., simple possession, shop theft under £500, low-level public order), directing offenders to NHS-commissioned Community Sentence Treatment Requirements (drug/alcohol/mental health), with 12–24 months of supervised treatment, random testing, electronic monitoring where proportionate, and restorative justice; breaches trigger swift, graduated sanctions and potential activation of a suspended custodial term; HMCTS, Probation Service, and local Integrated Care Boards to deliver fast-track assessments within 72 hours of conviction; funded by reallocating a portion of the MoJ prison operating budget to a ringfenced CSTR expansion.

Sentencing and Rehabilitation Reform Act: Codify whole-life orders and expanded minimum tariffs for specified serious violent and sexual offences and terrorism, while creating an earned-release framework for other prisoners that grants up to an additional 20% reduction in time in custody (beyond statutory release points) for completing accredited education, vocational qualifications, and offending-behaviour programmes; expand Release on Temporary Licence and employer partnerships to 25,000 placements per year, with mandatory victim-safety risk assessments and GPS tagging during ROTL; require every prison to offer guaranteed access to Level 2 literacy/numeracy and trade apprenticeships; Parole Board retains discretion and can revoke credits for misconduct.

Prison Estate Modernisation and Capacity Safety Plan: Authorise construction of four 1,500-place, rehabilitation-focused prisons modelled on Scandinavian regimes, paired with closure of eight highest-risk Victorian prisons within seven years; set a statutory officer-to-prisoner minimum ratio of 1:6 on daytime regimes, introduce in-cell digital education access, and fund a 15% pay uplift to reduce attrition; capital funded via a multi-year MoJ settlement and a temporary 0.1% surcharge on Crown Court fines; require independent evaluation of impacts on violence, self-harm, and reoffending, acknowledging that net capacity may increase by approximately 2,000 places during the transition.

State Sentencing Guidelines Reform: For first- and second-time nonviolent offenses (e.g., shoplifting under a set threshold, simple drug possession, low-level fraud), judges must impose a presumptive non-custodial sentence consisting of 12–18 months of electronic monitoring, nightly curfews, 20 hours/week of work or accredited education, mandatory victim restitution, and evidence-based treatment as needed. Custodial sentences require written findings of specific public-safety risk. Violations trigger graduated sanctions (increased monitoring, weekend custody), with automatic conversion to a custodial sentence after the third serious breach.

Violent Offender Accountability and Rehabilitation Act: Establish a statewide sentencing floor requiring repeat violent felons to serve at least 80% of their sentence in custody, while mandating that prisons provide accredited vocational training, cognitive-behavioral therapy, and trauma/substance-use treatment beginning within six months of intake. Parole eligibility requires successful program completion and a validated low-risk assessment. Upon release, high-risk individuals receive 24 months of intensive supervision with GPS monitoring and mandatory employment or training. The act funds secure therapeutic units and reentry services through dedicated appropriations and facility upgrades.

Corrections-to-Community Prevention Reinvestment Ordinance: Require counties to redirect 10% of annual jail operating budget growth into a dedicated fund for youth clubs, mentorship, after-school programs, apprenticeships, and violence-interruption services in high-incarceration neighborhoods, with free access and guaranteed evening/weekend hours. Awards are performance-based, tied to reductions in juvenile arrests and school truancy. The ordinance sets a minimum jail staffing floor and an automatic pause on new reinvestment if average jail occupancy exceeds 95% for 60 days. Annual independent audits and public dashboards report costs, participation, and recidivism outcomes.

State Corrections Rehabilitation and Staffing Modernization Act: mandate minimum officer-to-incarcerated-person staffing ratios of 1:8 in general population units; increase correctional officer base pay by 18% and establish a two-year training and certification standard; require every state prison to provide accredited GED, vocational, and cognitive behavioral therapy programs with participation slots for at least 70% of eligible inmates; tie wardens’ performance reviews to three-year postrelease recidivism metrics; sunset statewide use of electronic monitoring for low-risk offenders due to poor cost-effectiveness, with the savings and a 0.1% general fund supplement dedicated to in-prison rehabilitation services; no changes to sentencing lengths or release eligibility.

Sentencing Bifurcation Reform: reclassify first-time nonviolent drug possession and property offenses under $1,000 as presumptive noncustodial, substituting a 12–18 month community sentence combining electronic monitoring with curfews, weekly drug testing, and mandatory job training or education; expand specialty courts and cap jail time for technical probation violations at 7 days; simultaneously increase statutory maximums and create mandatory minimums for violent repeat offenses (e.g., +2 years for second felony gun offense, +5 years for third violent felony); set a target to reduce new prison admissions for nonviolent offenses by 25% over five years.

Maximum-Security Privilege Tightening and Youth Prevention Fund Pilot: for inmates in maximum-security and whole-life-tariff units, eliminate in-cell televisions, personal gaming devices, and streaming-ready tablets; restrict electronics access to supervised education labs and behavior-contingent communal rooms; standardize a stricter incentive system with loss of privileges for misconduct and earned access for sustained good behavior; dedicate audited savings to a ring-fenced Youth Crime Prevention Fund that expands after-school programs, apprenticeships, and summer jobs in high-crime neighborhoods; independent evaluation to report on institutional safety, misconduct rates, and fiscal impacts after 24 months.

Federal rehabilitation-first prison reform without population targets: require all state and federal prisons to adopt unit-based housing with a 1:8 officer-to-resident ratio, raise correctional officer base pay by 20% to address short-staffing, and deliver evidence-based education, vocational training, and cognitive-behavioral therapy at a minimum of 10 hours per week per incarcerated person; establish in-prison reentry centers that begin 12 months before release with guaranteed ID, housing placement, and job-matching services; award performance grants based on reductions in three-year reoffending rates rather than headcount; prohibit substituting incarceration with electronic tagging in lieu of programming; phased in over five years with independent evaluations.

State sentencing and diversion reform to reduce prison admissions for low-level, non-violent offenses: reclassify simple drug possession and property offenses under $1,500 as misdemeanors with presumptive community sanctions; implement police-led pre-booking diversion to treatment and restorative justice for eligible first- and second-time offenders; cap prison use for technical probation/parole violations at short, swift custodial stays (maximum three days) before graduated community responses; set a 25% reduction target in new prison admissions for these offenses within three years; fund expanded probation, treatment capacity, and specialized courts through justice-reinvestment of savings; require victim restitution and validated risk assessments to exclude high-risk or violent individuals; anticipate higher short-term probation caseloads and upfront costs.

City-county post-release supervision expansion with electronic monitoring: require moderate-risk felony releases to complete 6–12 months of GPS-based monitoring with curfews, exclusion zones around victims and high-risk locations, twice-weekly in-person check-ins, and immediate graduated sanctions for violations; pair monitoring with intensive case management, subsidized employment slots, and day-reporting centers to address criminogenic needs; create data minimization rules (retain location data no longer than 90 days unless tied to a criminal investigation) and establish an independent oversight board; fund the program via a dedicated public safety levy and state grants; acknowledge increased device and staffing costs and risks of false alerts, mitigated by 24/7 monitoring centers and clear violation thresholds.

England and Wales: Abolish custodial sentences of 12 months or less for non-violent, non-sexual offences and replace them with Community Rehabilitation Orders that combine mandatory unpaid work, targeted treatment (addiction and mental health), education, and electronic monitoring where indicated; require courts to use validated risk and needs assessments at sentencing; convert most technical probation breaches into graduated non-custodial sanctions rather than automatic recall; fund multi-agency local teams (probation, health, housing, employment) via outcome-based contracts tied to reduced reoffending; publish quarterly breach and compliance data. Tradeoffs include higher upfront spending on community services and increased supervision caseloads, with a risk of noncompliance requiring rapid response capacity.

UK Serious Harm Sentencing and Capacity Act: Impose whole-life tariffs with no parole for specified offences (e.g., murder with aggravating factors, terrorist acts causing death, serial rape) and mandatory 25-year minimums for repeat serious violent offenders; expand high-security prison capacity by 2,000 places to eliminate overcrowding and allow separation of high-risk inmates; ring-fence funding for accredited education, mental health, and vocational programs for eligible long-term prisoners; bar earned-time credits and early release for the specified offences; require annual independent inspections of prison safety and staffing ratios. Tradeoffs include significant capital and operating costs and reduced judicial discretion in exceptional cases.

England and Wales: Decriminalise simple possession of personal-use quantities of Class B and Class C drugs and replace criminal charges with civil sanctions and mandatory health assessments, with police-issued diversion notices requiring attendance at an NHS-led one-stop hub within seven days; model hub services on international best practice (e.g., Portugal), integrating addiction treatment, mental health care, and social support; completion of the program results in no criminal record; retain criminal penalties for supply, Class A possession, and possession in schools or prisons; run a five-year pilot in ten police force areas with independent evaluation and a sunset clause. Tradeoffs include upfront investment in treatment capacity and the possibility of mixed short-term public order impacts during transition.

State Sentencing Guidelines Reform: Adopt presumptive non-custodial sentences for non-violent felonies with offense severity levels 1–3 and all misdemeanors, replacing incarceration with 12–24 months of supervised community rehabilitation (drug treatment, cognitive behavioral therapy, job training/placement) and mandatory restitution; cap jail/prison time for technical probation/parole violations at graduated 3/7/14-day sanctions; mandate pre-sentence risk/needs assessments; reinvest 50% of net savings into county treatment providers and housing support; require a five-year sunset review tied to recidivism and cost benchmarks.

Prison Population Cap with Safety Valve: Enact a statutory cap at 95% of rated capacity for each state prison; when a facility reaches the cap, courts must use community sanctions, electronic monitoring, restorative justice, or fines for eligible non-violent offenses, while admissions are prioritized for violent and sexual offenses; establish an independent admissions triage commission, quarterly public reporting on capacity, and a victim-notification and judicial appeal process; authorize temporary emergency capacity only upon a declared security emergency with legislative review within 30 days.

Two-Tier Sentencing and Capacity Reallocation Act: Increase minimum sentences and restrict parole eligibility for repeat violent offenders (two or more qualifying violent felonies within 10 years), while simultaneously decriminalizing simple possession of controlled substances under two grams and first/second retail thefts under $300, replacing them with civil citations, mandatory clinical assessments, and targeted treatment; allocate $500 million over five years to modernize high-security units and $300 million to expand community treatment slots; require annual fiscal notes tracking whether diversion savings offset violent-incapacitation costs and publish independent evaluations of crime and prison population impacts.

Statewide Presumptive Community Supervision for Low-Risk Nonviolent Offenses: Judges must impose community supervision with GPS tagging (first 90 days), curfew, weekly check-ins, and mandatory enrollment in accredited GED/vocational programs for misdemeanors and nonviolent felonies scoring below a validated risk threshold; exclusions include domestic violence, sex offenses, firearm offenses, and repeat violent histories. Violations use graduated sanctions (swift, short custodial stays capped at 7 days), with revocation only after repeated noncompliance. Funds are shifted from corrections to hire community supervision officers at a 1:40 caseload cap and to purchase training seats; five-year sunset with independent evaluation and public reporting.

Justice Reinvestment Upstream Investment Mandate: By statute, a minimum of 20% of verified annual Department of Corrections savings from reduced incarceration (e.g., unit closures, shorter average stays) is redirected to place-based anti-poverty initiatives in census tracts with the highest incarceration rates. Eligible uses include Housing First vouchers, early childhood education slots, paid youth summer jobs, community mental health clinics, and apprenticeship wage subsidies, administered via performance-based contracts tied to reductions in arrests, felony filings, and jail bookings. An oversight board co-chaired by the Attorney General and State Budget Director certifies savings and triggers clawbacks if targets are missed.

Violent Crime Incapacitation and Nonviolent Earned Release Act: Creates a two-track framework under which specified violent felonies (e.g., homicide, aggravated sexual assault, armed robbery) require serving at least 85% of the sentence with no electronic monitoring substitution, while nonviolent offenses receive presumptive parole at 60% with up to 35% earned-time credits for completing accredited education, CBT, and industry-recognized apprenticeships. Establishes independent risk hearings for violent cases, expands in-prison education seats by 50%, and funds reentry navigators to secure IDs, housing, and employment offers prior to release; annual public safety impact and capacity reports required.

Introduce a national network of Problem-Solving Courts diverting eligible non-violent offenders with substance dependence or severe mental illness from custody into 12-24 month Treatment and Accountability Orders: mandatory NHS-delivered treatment, daily check-ins, curfew and electronic monitoring, random testing, education or employment placement, and fortnightly judicial reviews; graduated sanctions (including brief custodial stays) for non-compliance; a statutory presumption against remand for eligible cases; ring-fenced reallocation of 10% of projected prison capital spend to community treatment, supported housing and caseworkers; independent evaluation and public dashboards on completion and reoffending.

Secure Capacity and Reintegration Programme: fund 5,000 additional prison places (including 2,000 Category D open-prison places) to relieve overcrowding and expand work-release; set minimum officer-to-prisoner staffing ratios; require every prisoner to complete accredited education, addiction treatment where indicated, and a reintegration plan co-authored by a multi-agency 'Through-the-Gate' team (prison, probation, police, council, NHS, family support services); provide time-limited family support grants upon release; prohibit population-based early-release quotas; introduce tougher minimum sentences for repeat knife and serious burglary offences; link a portion of prison budgets to post-release employment and reoffending outcomes.

Adopt Restorative Community Reparation Sentencing: for non-violent offences causing local harm (e.g., criminal damage, shoplifting under £1,000, theft from vehicles), courts must first consider Restorative Community Service Orders of 300-800 hours of high-visibility repair work in affected areas, offender-funded restitution plans, and victim-offender conferencing where appropriate; orders include evening curfews with electronic monitoring and mandatory skills training; breaches convert to custodial sentences; Police and Crime Commissioners commission projects; savings from reduced custody are retained by local authorities to reinvest in prevention.

England and Wales Sentencing Council to adopt a 'Presumption Against Custody for Short Sentences' guideline: for non-violent offences with a guideline custodial term of 12 months or less, courts must impose a community order or suspended sentence with conditions (drug/alcohol treatment, mental health support, curfew and electronic monitoring, unpaid work, and restorative justice), unless they give written exceptional reasons; exclusions apply to domestic abuse, stalking, knife/weapon possession, child-related offences, and breach of restraining orders; HMCTS will expand problem-solving courts to supervise compliance, and HM Prison & Probation Service will redirect at least 20% of savings to local treatment and reoffending reduction services, with automatic record-sealing 24 months after successful completion.

Home Office and DHSC to implement a 'Health-Led Drug Possession Diversion' scheme: personal possession of small quantities (e.g., up to 3 days’ supply) of Class B and C drugs is reclassified as a civil infraction; police issue a diversion notice requiring a rapid assessment at a local Drug and Alcohol Hub, completion of treatment or education waives the civil penalty and triggers conditional expungement; 10 pilots of supervised consumption facilities, expanded naloxone distribution, and medication-assisted treatment are funded via a ringfenced transfer from the prison estate budget to local public health (OHID), alongside transitional housing slots tied to treatment; outcomes are independently evaluated after three years to determine national rollout.

Prison Capacity and Serious Harm Prioritisation Act: set a statutory safe operating cap for the prison estate (e.g., 95% of inspected capacity) and require that when the cap is reached, courts must sentence non-violent property and drug offenders to intensive community supervision with restitution, electronic monitoring, and vocational training unless a judge records exceptional risk; simultaneously, create longer minimum tariffs and dedicated high-security units for specified serious violent and sexual offences, expand in-prison education and accredited rehabilitation, and close unfit Victorian-era prisons with reinvestment into probation staffing, 'through-the-gate' resettlement, and employer apprenticeship pipelines for those released.

State Community Accountability Sentencing Reform: For first- or second-time nonviolent felonies involving less than $1,500 in loss, simple drug possession, and low-level fraud, judges must impose noncustodial sentences (12-24 months of community service, mandatory treatment, job training, and restitution through a verified payment plan). Successful completion reduces the conviction; violations trigger short custodial weekends capped at 14 days total. Exclusions cover domestic violence, weapon involvement, and organized theft. The statute closes one medium-security facility within 24 months and redirects $120M per year in savings to expand probation staffing, treatment slots, and victim restitution funds.

Federal Humane Prison Capacity and Standards Act: Establish enforceable national minimum standards requiring single-occupancy cells for sentenced prisoners by year 5, minimum square footage, climate control, 6 hours per day of education or therapy, and independent healthcare oversight. Authorize $8B in matching grants for states to renovate and construct facilities to eliminate overcrowding and meet standards, require 10 percent capacity buffers and ban triple-bunking, and tie funding to quarterly audits and corrective action plans. Sentencing lengths remain unchanged; noncompliant systems can be placed under temporary federal receivership.

State Focused Incapacitation and Supervision Swap: Abolish prison time for nonviolent misdemeanors and technical probation or parole violations, replacing them with graduated sanctions (electronic monitoring, day reporting, curfews, and treatment), while simultaneously imposing no-parole terms for repeat violent felonies and gun-involved crimes. Create 30 percent earned-time credits for nonviolent felonies tied to education and work. Fund 24-7 supervision centers and GPS monitoring via a surcharge on violent offender sentences, reserving prison beds for high-risk violent offenders and projecting a 15 percent prison population reduction over five years.

State Diversion and Multi-Agency Rehabilitation Pilot: authorize magistrates and probation to sentence first- and second-time nonviolent offenders (excluding offenses involving weapons, sexual harm, or serious injury) to 12 to 18 months of community-based rehabilitation delivered through local justice hubs co-staffed by probation, health, housing, and employment services; require a validated risk and needs assessment; set strict compliance conditions (weekly check-ins, drug testing where indicated, electronic attendance tracking); noncompliance triggers graduated sanctions and, after three material breaches, an automatic custodial backup sentence; fund hubs by redirecting 25 percent of projected prison expansion funds; sunset after five years with an independent cost-benefit and reoffending evaluation.

National Proportionate Sentencing and In-Prison Rehabilitation Upgrade: enact guideline reforms to align penalties with harm and culpability (for example, cap custodial terms for nonviolent property and drug possession at 24 months absent aggravation, and add aggravation matrices for repeat violent offenses); require all prisons to provide accredited education, vocational training, substance-use and mental-health programs with participation mandatory and tied to earned-time credits of up to 15 percent for nonviolent offenses; retain truth-in-sentencing for violent and sexual offenses at a minimum 85 percent time served; expand correctional staffing and program capacity with a dedicated capital fund; create judicial sentence review panels to correct outlier sentences that exceed guideline ranges.

Probation and Parole Technical Violation Reform: prohibit revocation to prison for first and second technical violations (missed appointment, curfew, positive test) absent a new criminal offense; implement a statewide graduated sanctions and incentives grid (warnings, increased reporting, day reporting centers, short community service stints, and earned discharge for sustained compliance); cap jail stays for technical violations at three days within any 90-day period; require transportation assistance and digital check-in options to reduce barriers; publish quarterly compliance and recidivism dashboards; reallocate court time saved to focus on violent and high-risk cases.

A state law decriminalizes possession of under 2 grams of most controlled substances for adults, replacing arrest with a mandatory clinical assessment within 72 hours and a tailored treatment or harm-reduction plan; completion results in no criminal record and automatic sealing. Counties receive formula grants to expand outpatient treatment, medication-assisted therapy, and supportive housing, funded by reallocating 20% of projected corrections budget growth and savings from reduced jail bookings. Police are trained and authorized to deflect eligible individuals to 24/7 drop-off centers instead of jail. Noncompliance triggers graduated administrative sanctions, not incarceration, except when a new violent offense occurs. The law sunsets in 6 years unless independent evaluation shows equal or improved public safety and reduced recidivism.

A federal matching-grant program requires states to cap prison occupancy at 95% of rated capacity within 3 years, with compliance tied to funding for new construction and retrofits that meet minimum humane standards: single- or double-occupancy cells of at least 60 square feet per person, 14 hours weekly of evidence-based programming, a 1:64 custody staff ratio, and on-site mental health clinicians. States must phase out long-term solitary confinement beyond 15 consecutive days, install independent correctional ombuds offices, and separate high-risk violent offenders using secure but program-rich units. Noncompliant facilities face intake freezes and federal receivership. The program increases near-term capital and operating costs but reduces overcrowding and safety incidents.

A state Two-Track Sentencing Reform sets presumptive community sentences for nonviolent felonies and misdemeanors, substituting up to 1,000 hours of verified community service, electronic monitoring with curfews, and mandatory substance-use or cognitive-behavioral therapy, with jail prohibited for technical violations absent a new criminal charge; simultaneously, it creates mandatory minimum prison terms of 7 to 12 years for repeat violent felony offenses and gun-involved robberies or assaults, with parole eligibility only after completion of intensive rehabilitation modules and demonstrated risk reduction. Judges may depart from mandatory minimums only upon a unanimous three-judge review citing exceptional circumstances. Annual public reports track impacts on prison population, costs, and violent crime.

Parliament to legislate a presumption against custodial sentences under 6 months in England and Wales, with the Sentencing Council revising guidelines so eligible cases receive suspended sentence orders or community orders combining 80–200 hours of unpaid work, income‑adjusted fines, curfews with electronic monitoring (up to 12 months), and mandatory rehabilitation/education modules; two proven breaches trigger automatic activation of the suspended term absent exceptional circumstances; probation staffing increased by 30% and a national compliance unit created to enforce conditions.

National Drug Possession Diversion and Decriminalisation Act: reclassify personal possession of small quantities of Class A–C drugs as a civil infraction; police issue a health‑referral citation instead of arrest; NHS assessment within 14 days with a tailored treatment/education plan; custodial sentences barred for possession‑only; no criminal record or DNA retention upon completion; automatic expungement of prior possession convictions after 12 months offense‑free; £250m per year ring‑fenced for local diversion hubs and treatment capacity.

HM Prison and Probation Service Minimum Standards and Capacity Relief Programme: by statute, require at least 8 hours out‑of‑cell time daily and 15 hours per week of accredited education or work in every prison by 2028; recruit 5,000 additional officers and 2,000 educators; commission two new Category C resettlement prisons and convert three existing sites to open conditions to decant overcrowded Victorian estates; cap occupancy at certified normal accommodation and tie funding to independent inspection ratings, accepting short‑term capital costs and operational disruption during decanting.

State Prison Population Reduction and Diversion Act: Within five years, reduce the state prison population by 25% through a statutory presumption against incarceration for nonviolent, low-level offenses; mandatory prosecutor-offered diversion for first-time offenders; replacement of short custodial terms with day-fines, community service, treatment, and electronic monitoring; a ban on prison admissions for technical probation/parole violations; and reallocation of 20% of corrections budgets to county-level probation, substance-use and mental-health services, and housing supports, with quarterly public reporting and a seven-year sunset clause.

National Violent Recidivist Accountability and Sentencing Reform: Establish a 15-year mandatory minimum for a second violent felony within 10 years and a 25-year minimum for a third; limit parole eligibility to the final 10% of the sentence for covered offenses; require secure separation units to prevent mixing of low-level and high-risk inmates; and mandate in-prison education and cognitive-behavioral programs for all eligible inmates, funded by redirection of resources from reduced parole supervision caseloads.

State Earned-Time and Reentry Acceleration Program: Allow nonviolent inmates to earn up to a 40% sentence reduction through completion of accredited education, vocational training, addiction and mental-health treatment, and restorative-justice agreements; provide six months of transitional housing, a wage subsidy for employers hiring participants, and automatic record-sealing for qualifying offenses after two years of compliance; exclude serious violent and sex offenses; and require an independent evaluation of recidivism and cost savings after three years.

Presumption of community orders with GPS tagging for short sentences: Replace custodial sentences of 12 months or less (excluding violent, sexual, stalking, and domestic abuse offences) with a presumptive community order that includes GPS tagging with a nightly curfew, 150–300 hours of supervised unpaid work tied to local community improvement, and mandatory education or employment training. Breach responses follow a graduated scale culminating in a maximum 28-day custodial sanction for repeated non-compliance. Courts must record reasons to override the presumption. HM Prison and Probation Service will expand a 24/7 monitoring hub and add 1,000 probation officers, with an independent evaluation reporting reoffending and compliance outcomes after 24 months.

Serious Violence Sentencing and Rehabilitation Reform Act: Introduce statutory minimum custodial terms for GBH with intent, knife-enabled robbery, and repeat violent offenders; end automatic halfway release for these offences and require prisoners to earn up to 20% sentence reduction through accredited behavioural programmes and vocational qualifications. Fund 2,500 additional modern prison places, recruit 3,000 officers, and create employer-backed in-prison apprenticeship workshops in construction, logistics, and digital support. Parole decisions must consider completion of programmes and victim safety plans. Capital cost £1.2bn over four years, partly offset by reduced recall rates via improved resettlement services.

Health-led diversion and civil penalties for personal drug possession: Reclassify simple personal possession of Class B and C drugs to a civil offence handled outside criminal courts, issuing a £150–£300 fixed penalty plus mandatory NHS clinical assessment and up to 12 months of community-based treatment where indicated; criminal charges apply only after a third non-compliant incident within two years. Police must offer on-the-spot referral to Liaison and Diversion services; successful completion expunges the record after 12 months. Allocate £250m to expand NHS addiction services and local recovery housing, financed by projected savings from reduced court and prison caseloads.

National Presumption of Noncustodial Sentencing for Nonviolent Low-Level Offences: Parliament enacts a Sentencing Reform Act requiring courts to impose community-based sanctions (probation with mandatory education/drug treatment, restorative justice conferencing, day fines linked to income, electronic monitoring) for first- and second-time nonviolent offences (e.g., simple drug possession, shoplifting under £500, fare evasion), with custody permitted only after written findings of specified aggravating factors (weapon use, organised crime involvement, repeated noncompliance). Successful completion triggers automatic record-sealing after 12 months; violations result in swift, graduated sanctions short of prison. Probation services receive performance-based funding tied to reduced reoffending.

Serious Harm Sentencing and Rehabilitation Act: The UK establishes statutory minimum custodial sentences and restricted parole for defined Category A violent and sexual offences (murder, rape, terrorism, aggravated knife crime), including a 25-year minimum-to-parole for murder and life-without-parole for multiple murders. All other offences become eligible for expanded earned-release credits (up to 33% sentence reduction) contingent on completion of accredited education, vocational training, and victim-awareness programmes. £500m is ringfenced to expand in-prison training workshops and apprenticeships. A Public Safety Panel composed of senior judges and victims’ representatives reviews any exceptional early release for Category A cases after the minimum term.

Legally Binding Local Jail Population Caps with Remand Reform: In England and Wales, statutory caps are set for each local remand and short-sentence facility based on safe staffing and humane standards; when a cap is reached, courts must prioritise non-custodial sentences and pretrial release for low-risk defendants using validated risk assessments, supervised release, and electronic monitoring. Remand is reserved for cases with clear and present risk of serious harm or strong, evidenced flight risk, and courts must issue written reasons for any remand decision. Court reminder systems, travel assistance, and rapid hearing scheduling are mandated to reduce failures to appear. An independent inspectorate audits compliance quarterly; temporary cap exceptions require ministerial authorisation during declared emergencies.

State Presumptive Noncustodial Sentencing Act: For nonviolent misdemeanors and low-level felonies (no weapon, no injury, loss under $5,000), the default sentence is community supervision with conditions (treatment, restitution, job training) and up to 30 days of jail only as a 'swift, certain, and fair' sanction for violations; prison is prohibited for technical probation violations; a validated risk assessment may inform, but not be the sole basis for, any custodial decision; 50% of savings from reduced imprisonment are earmarked for county supervision, treatment capacity, and victim services; the policy sunsets in 5 years pending independent evaluation of reoffending and costs.

Federal Violent Crime Accountability and Rehabilitation Act: Require persons convicted of specified violent offenses to serve at least 85-100% of their imposed sentence (truth-in-sentencing), reduce overcrowding by funding facility modernization and staffing to meet national safety standards, and mandate 8 hours per day of evidence-based programming (education, cognitive behavioral therapy, vocational training) for all incarcerated people; expand Pell Grant eligibility and reentry planning beginning at intake; limit early release to nonviolent cases with verified program completion; create an independent inspector general to audit safety, programming quality, and victim notification practices.

State Personal-Use Drug Reform and Deflection Policy: Reclassify simple possession of small quantities of controlled substances for personal use as a civil violation with mandatory clinical assessment and referral to treatment; require health-based citations instead of arrest at the point of contact; apply the change retroactively with automatic record sealing for qualifying past convictions; convert failure to complete assessment into a means-tested fine, with repeated noncompliance eligible for misdemeanor drug court; fund community treatment capacity and mobile crisis teams with cannabis tax revenue; publish annual public reports on overdose trends, recidivism, and treatment access.

State 'Truth-in-Sentencing and Rehabilitation Standards Act': require people convicted of designated violent felonies to serve at least 85% of their imposed sentence, eliminate blanket early-release credits for those crimes, and fund mandatory, accredited in-prison programs (cognitive behavioral therapy, substance use treatment, GED, and industry-recognized vocational training) with per-prison performance benchmarks; create a sentencing commission to recalibrate offense-level guidelines to better match harm and culpability without reducing penalties for violent offenses; expand correctional staffing and facility space to end overcrowding and allow full-day programming; require annual public recidivism and program outcome audits by an independent evaluator.

Statewide Presumptive Diversion and Reclassification Reform: reclassify simple possession of small quantities of controlled substances and low-level property offenses under $1,000 as misdemeanors with a presumptive sentence of probation, treatment, and restitution instead of prison; create county-operated treatment courts with statutory authority to mandate medication-assisted treatment and job placement; prohibit prison as a sentencing option for first and second convictions of these offenses absent documented high risk of violent reoffending; cap jail time for noncompliance at 7 days with graduated sanctions; automatically seal records 12 months after successful completion; dedicate 50% of avoided incarceration costs to expand community treatment capacity.

Earned-Time Credits and Risk-Based Parole Expansion: authorize up to 25% sentence reduction for nonviolent inmates who complete tiered evidence-based programs (education, vocational certification, cognitive behavioral therapy) and maintain clean disciplinary records; expand parole eligibility for nonviolent offenses at the earliest statutory date with mandatory electronic monitoring and curfew for the first 90 days; adopt a statewide violation response matrix that prefers swift, certain, and brief sanctions over full revocation and bars prison returns for technical violations beyond 30 days; require a portion of savings to fund victim services, parole officer caseload reduction, and analytics to track reoffending rates by program.

A national law mandating evidence-based rehabilitation in all prisons, funded by increasing correctional officer pay and staffing to accreditation benchmarks, expanding in-prison education, vocational apprenticeships with employer partnerships, cognitive behavioral therapy, and addiction/mental-health treatment; requiring every facility to provide at least 20 hours per week of programming to eligible inmates; tying warden compensation to reductions in post-release reoffending; and establishing independent audits, with no targets to reduce the prison population.

A state sentencing-guideline overhaul that creates presumptive noncustodial sanctions for first- and second-time nonviolent offenses (e.g., personal-use drug possession, shoplifting under $1,500, simple fraud), expands problem-solving courts, mandates restorative justice and community service, and caps jail time for technical probation violations at 7 days per incident and 21 days per year; requires validated risk assessment and victim input; reinvests prison savings into county-run supervision, housing, and treatment; and sets a target of a 25% reduction in new prison admissions over five years with annual public safety audits.

A state Violent Repeat Offender Sentencing Floor and Parole Reform statute that sets mandatory minimum terms for second violent felony convictions (e.g., minimum 5–10 years depending on offense) and requires at least 85% of sentenced time be served before eligibility for release, while simultaneously expanding in-prison rehabilitation and reentry planning; appropriates funds to prevent overcrowding by adding capacity and raising officer pay; and mandates five-year reviews of recidivism and costs to adjust the policy if needed.

National Tiered Regime and Serious Violence Sentencing Act: increase statutory minimums and presumptive sentences for repeat violent and sexual offenses by 20–30%; remove non-educational electronic entertainment (TVs, gaming consoles, personal tablets) from high-security prisons and restrict privileges for whole-life-tariff inmates to essentials; expand earned-credit programs that reduce sentences up to 20% for nonviolent offenders who complete accredited education/vocational programs and maintain infraction-free records; earmark 1% of the corrections budget for youth employment, evening recreation, and truancy interventions to reduce future admissions.

State sentencing guideline reform replacing all custodial sentences of 12 months or less (excluding domestic violence and stalking) with Intensive Community Accountability Orders: GPS monitoring, nightly 8 p.m.–6 a.m. curfew, 20 hours/week community service, weekly probation check-ins, mandatory treatment where indicated, and enforceable restitution; violations trigger swift, certain 24–72 hour jail stays; completion earns automatic record sealing for eligible first-time offenders; target a 25% reduction in local jail populations within two years.

State-level decriminalization of possession of small quantities of controlled substances (e.g., <2 grams) and creation of mandatory health-diversion dockets: police issue civil citations and immediate referral to treatment navigators; first- and second-time nonviolent property offenses under $1,000 routed to restorative justice panels with binding restitution agreements; failure to comply activates a suspended custodial sentence; redirect $50 million in annual incarceration savings to treatment capacity, housing stabilization, and victim compensation funds.

State Truth-in-Sentencing Rehabilitation Investment Act: require people convicted of felonies to serve at least 85% of imposed sentences, prohibit early-release quotas, raise correctional officer base pay by 20% with minimum staffing ratios, and mandate accredited cognitive-behavioral, education, and vocational programs throughout custody; phase out electronic ankle monitoring as a post-conviction alternative to incarceration (permitted only for narrowly defined pretrial cases with individualized judicial findings) and redirect the savings to in-prison rehabilitation and staff training.

Sentencing Proportionality and Community Accountability Reform: establish an independent state sentencing commission to recalibrate guidelines so penalties align with offense harm and risk; create presumptive non-custodial sentences (probation with day-reporting, restitution, treatment, and victim-offender mediation where appropriate) for first-time nonviolent misdemeanors and low-level felonies under a $1,000 loss threshold absent aggravating factors; repeal mandatory minimums for simple drug possession and minor property offenses; require swift-and-certain sanctions (2–7 day custodial stays) for supervision violations; bar routine use of ankle monitors in favor of in-person check-ins and employment verification; include a five-year sunset with independent evaluation of recidivism and costs.

Rehabilitative Capacity Expansion and Facility Modernization Program: issue state bonds to replace overcapacity legacy prisons with smaller, rehabilitation-focused facilities (250–500 beds) that provide normalized housing, on-site education and trades labs, therapeutic communities, and low inmate-to-staff ratios; implement a staffing plan with a 15% pay premium to recruit credentialed treatment professionals and correctional officers; close two obsolete facilities to fund operations at the new sites; maintain current admission and release policies while publishing annual independent audits on recidivism, in-custody safety, and cost per offender.

Introduce a statutory presumption against custodial sentences under 12 months in England and Wales, replacing them with Intensive Community Orders that combine 20–30 hours per week of unpaid work, a nightly electronic curfew, compulsory education or vocational training, treatment for addiction or mental health needs, and income-adjusted day fines; exceptions limited to offences causing serious harm or offenders assessed as high risk; require restorative justice where victims consent; direct the Sentencing Council to revise guidelines accordingly; shift funding from prisons to probation and local providers; manage breaches via an escalating sanctions grid that increases curfew intensity and unpaid work and only permits short custody after repeated non-compliance.

Enact a Prison Capacity and Decency Act that sets a legally binding 95 percent occupancy cap across the prison estate and funds a seven-year capital programme to build five small regional Category C or D prisons and fully refurbish vulnerable high-security sites; mandate minimum standards of at least eight hours per day out of cell, access to accredited rehabilitation programmes, and a 1:4 officer-to-prisoner ratio on residential units; require HMPPS to end 23-hour lockdowns and install in-cell telephony and tablets for education; authorise temporary modular units to meet the cap during construction; empower the inspectorate to enforce compliance and close non-compliant wings; finance via a small hypothecated National Insurance rise with ring-fenced staffing and training budgets.

Create a Serious Harm Sentencing and Supervision regime under which adults convicted of a second specified violent or sexual offence within ten years must receive an Extended Determinate Sentence with at least 80 percent of the term served in custody and release only by Parole Board certification; end automatic halfway release for these cases; require annual risk-review hearings, completion of intensive offending-behaviour programmes, and MAPPA Level 2–3 supervision for five years post-release; define the specified list to exclude lower-harm offences to avoid net-widening; include a statutory five-year sunset review due to projected impacts on prison population and costs.

A state legislature enacts a Tiered Sentencing and Incentive Act that: increases statutory minimums by 25% for specified violent felonies; eliminates personal electronics and gaming devices for inmates serving sentences longer than 25 years while maintaining secure education-only tablets; expands earned-time credits up to 15% for completion of accredited education, substance-use treatment, and prison industries work (excluding homicide and sex offenses from early release); and appropriates $50 million annually for youth apprenticeships, after-school programs, and targeted job training in high-arrest ZIP codes, with annual public reporting on prison misconduct, program completion, and violent crime trends.

A state adopts presumptive diversion for first- and second-time nonviolent offenses (e.g., simple drug possession, retail theft under $750, trespass, fare evasion), requiring judges to assign a 6–12 month community plan combining cognitive behavioral therapy, substance-use treatment (including medication-assisted treatment where indicated), job placement, community service, and victim restitution; successful completion triggers automatic record sealing and dismissal, while noncompliance results in graduated sanctions and, only after repeated failures, short custodial stays; the policy reallocates $30 million from closing one underutilized prison unit to expand probation staffing and certified treatment providers, with a statewide dashboard tracking completion and reoffending.

A statewide supervision reform caps incarceration for technical probation/parole violations (missed check-ins, curfew breaches, positive drug tests) at swift, short stays of 3, 7, and 15 days per episode with a 30-day annual maximum, reserves prison terms for new criminal conduct or absconding, and pairs conditions with GPS monitoring where needed, mandatory employment or education enrollment, and victim restitution; individuals earn 20 days of early termination credit for each violation-free month; savings from reduced prison bed-days fund additional officers, electronic monitoring, and treatment slots, with an independent audit of outcomes after three years.

State Sentencing Reform and Diversion Act: For non-violent drug possession and low-value property offenses under a defined threshold, courts must impose community-based sanctions instead of incarceration, including 12–18 months of probation with medication-assisted treatment where clinically indicated, cognitive-behavioral therapy, regular drug testing that tapers with compliance, job placement services, and victim-offender mediation when appropriate. Successful completion triggers automatic record sealing. Violations receive swift, graduated 2–7 day custodial sanctions but no full revocation absent a new crime. At least 50% of avoided incarceration costs are statutorily redirected to local addiction treatment, housing, and mental health clinics in high-incarceration neighborhoods.

Integrated Public Safety and Reentry Partnership Act: Expand open-prison capacity by 20% for lower-risk prisoners with day-release for work and education; require a verified reentry plan six months before release; fund licensed family therapists to provide mandatory pre- and post-release family reintegration sessions; create joint police–probation neighborhood supervision teams; establish a statewide program that pays vetted ex-prisoners to deliver school-based prevention talks; increase penalties for in-prison assaults and contraband smuggling to reinforce order; and mandate at least 12 months of post-release supervision with graduated responses. Appropriations include additional resources for police, prison staffing, and community supervision.

Capacity Relief through Home Confinement and Earned Time: When state prisons exceed design capacity, automatically shift eligible non-violent inmates within nine months of release to GPS-monitored home confinement with curfews, work or education requirements, and randomized substance testing. Expand earned-time credits up to 30% of sentence length for completion of accredited treatment, education, and vocational programs. Prohibit incarceration for technical probation and parole violations, substituting community sanctions and mandated treatment. Use a validated risk assessment to exclude high-risk individuals. Publish annual recidivism and cost-savings reports, dedicating savings to pretrial services and victim support funds.
